nodes.label: Hand quern
nodes.desc: Grain ground by hand between stones. A person grinds a few kg of grain an hour [M]. It went on beside the mill, often illegally, for centuries.

nodes.label: Suit of mill and multure
nodes.desc: The lord's monopoly on grinding: tenants had to use his mill and pay multure, often a sixteenth to a twentieth of the grain [M]. The first rent on shared capital, with about 6,000 mills in 1086 and perhaps 10,000 by 1300 [V]. One of the main frictions between lords and tenants.

nodes.label: Zaan wind sawmill
nodes.desc: Cornelis Corneliszoon's wind-driven sawmill of 1592 turned the windmill to industry. The Zaan had 600 to 1,000 windmills at its peak, over 200 of them sawmills [V]; they cut Baltic logs into boards for shipyards.

nodes.label: Hay meadow
nodes.desc: Mown grassland that fed draught beasts through winter. A horse's year of hay came from 1.5 to 2 acres (0.6 to 0.8 ha) [V]. Meadow was land that could not also grow bread.

nodes.label: Fodder oats
nodes.desc: Grain grown for horses rather than people. A hard-worked 19th-century horse ate 12 to 16 lb of grain and 12 lb of hay a day [V], roughly 2 to 3 ha of land per horse [C]. England's horses ate the produce of perhaps a fifth of the farmland [M].

nodes.label: Collar-harnessed horse
nodes.desc: A horse with a padded collar and iron shoes, in Europe from about the 10th century [M]: about 500 to 750 W, half again as fast as an ox, but it needs oats [M]. Oxen still outnumbered horses about two to one on English demesnes at the end of the 14th century; peasants took to the horse faster [V].

nodes.label: Straw, dung and furze fuel
nodes.desc: Farm by-products burned where wood was short. They burn fast, and every load of dung burned is manure lost to the fields. National accounts count them poorly, which is part of why rural English fuel per head reads as low as 0.5 t of wood [V].

nodes.label: City firewood ring
nodes.desc: The ring of coppice that heated a medieval city. London burned about 141,000 tons of wood fuel a year c.1300 [V], carted by land up to about 18 to 20 km [V]; [C] some 45,000 to 55,000 ha of coppice under rotation.

nodes.label: Sea coal, Tyne to London
nodes.desc: Coal from outcrops near the Tyne shipped to London: for lime-burning and smithing from the 13th century, household fuel from the later 16th [V]. Coal gave half of England's energy by 1700 and over 90% by 1850 [V].

nodes.label: Chimney and enclosed hearth
nodes.desc: A brick or stone flue that let houses have upper floors and waste less fuel; it spread in England in the 16th century [M]. An open hearth delivered perhaps 10 to 20% of its heat to the room [M].

nodes.label: Coal grate
nodes.desc: An iron grate and tall chimney for burning coal at home, from the late 16th century in London where coal was cheap by water [V]. Coal needed new grates, chimneys and processes before it could replace wood [V].

nodes.label: Rushlight
nodes.desc: Rush pith dipped in kitchen fat: the cheapest made light, open to any household with fat. For most of history the evening was rationed by fat.

nodes.label: Tallow candle
nodes.desc: Tallow from cattle and sheep on a wick of cotton or linen; a chandler's trade in towns, and smoky. Beeswax candles were for the Church and the rich.

nodes.label: Oil lamp
nodes.desc: A wick in vegetable or animal oil: olive oil in the south, rapeseed and linseed in the north, whale oil from the 17th to 19th centuries. It paid where oil was cheaper than tallow.

nodes.label: Whaling for lamp oil
nodes.desc: Whale oil joined light to a global hunt from the 17th century [M]. Kerosene ended its lamp market in the 1860s [M].

nodes.label: Town gas lighting
nodes.desc: Coal baked for gas, piped to street and house lamps; London's Gas Light and Coke Company from 1812 [M]. It joined light to the coal chain and city pipes, and its coal tar became dyes and drugs.

nodes.label: Kerosene refining
nodes.desc: Crude oil distilled for lamp kerosene from the 1860s [M], after the Titusville well of 1859 [M]. It ended whale oil's lamp market; petrol and diesel came later from the same stills.

nodes.label: Petrol and diesel
nodes.desc: Lighter and heavier cuts of crude oil, first a waste of the kerosene trade, then the fuel of engines. They made the car, the tractor and the aeroplane.

nodes.label: Electric light
nodes.desc: Lamps fed by wire from central stations, from 1882 (Pearl Street, Holborn Viaduct) [M]. Four separate light chains (herds, bees, whales, coal) collapsed into one network that also drove motors and trams.

nodes.label: Potash (wood-ash lye)
nodes.place: every wooded region; later the Baltic and North America
nodes.desc: Wood ash leached to lye: the alkali of glass, soap, bleaching and dyeing. The Spiegelberg glassworks needed about 800 centners a year, some 40,000 m3 of wood [V]. Ash-burning competed with hearths and ironworks for the woods.

nodes.label: Kelp and barilla ash
nodes.desc: Soda ash from burned seaweed (kelp) and Spanish saltwort (barilla) [M]. With wood ash, one of three land- and shore-based alkali chains that the Leblanc process replaced.

nodes.label: Forest glass
nodes.desc: Glass fluxed with beech ash: Theophilus (c.1100) gives two parts ash to one of quartz, and with furnace fuel 150 to 200 kg of wood per kg of glass [V]. The works moved with the forest.

nodes.label: Coal-fired glass
nodes.desc: English glass moved to coal after the 1615 ban on wood for glass furnaces [M]; coal-fired furnaces made glass bottles in 17th-century England [M]. It joined containers to the coal chain.

nodes.label: Laws preserving the woods
nodes.desc: State rules for fuel against timber: the 1543 Act for the Preservation of Woods [M] and bans on wood in glass furnaces (1615) [M]. They pushed fuel-hungry trades toward coal.

nodes.label: Soap boiling
nodes.desc: Fat (tallow, oil) boiled with lye from wood ash, later with soda. A soap-boiler competed with glassworks and hearths for wood and with chandlers for fat.

nodes.label: Leblanc soda
nodes.desc: Soda made from salt, sulphuric acid and coal (1790s) [M]. Three land-based alkali chains (wood ash, kelp, barilla) became one chemical chain fed by salt, coal and stone, and the old ash trades died.

nodes.label: Solvay soda
nodes.desc: Soda from salt, limestone and ammonia (1860s) [M]; cleaner and cheaper than Leblanc, which it displaced.

nodes.label: Chlorine bleaching
nodes.desc: Bleach from salt-derived chlorine in place of weeks of sun and lye. It merged the salt chain with the chains for textiles and bleach that had run on wood ash.

nodes.label: Briquetage salt pots
nodes.desc: Brine boiled dry in coarse clay pots that were broken to get the salt out; Iron Age Droitwich worked this way [M].

nodes.label: Brine boiling in lead pans
nodes.desc: Near-saturated brine boiled over wood in lead pans: four tons of brine gave a ton of salt [V]. Droitwich burned about 6,000 loads of wood a year in the 1530s [V], brought from Worcester, Bromsgrove and Alcester. A chokepoint (salt) bound to distant woods.

nodes.label: Fuel rent for salt
nodes.desc: Manors owed the salt works wood in return for salt: Martin Hussingtree owed 100 cartloads a year for a set quantity [V]. A chokepoint tied to its sink at a distance by rent in kind.

nodes.label: Bay salt (solar pans)
nodes.desc: Sea salt made by the sun in coastal pans; seawater is about 3.5% salt [M], too weak to boil cheaply. Atlantic bay salt undersold boiled salt for fish-curing [M].

nodes.label: Cheshire rock salt, coal pans
nodes.desc: From the 17th century rock salt and coal-fired pans joined the salt chain to the coal chain [M]. In the 19th century salt became the feedstock of soda and chlorine.

nodes.label: Malt
nodes.desc: Barley steeped, sprouted and dried on a floor and kiln. It made ale and beer (a staple drink and much of a household's calories [M]), vinegar and spirits.

nodes.label: Hopped beer
nodes.desc: Beer with hops, which keeps and travels where ale soured; in England from the 15th century [M]. It let brewing grow from the household to the town brewhouse.

nodes.label: Coopered barrels
nodes.desc: Oak staves and iron or withy hoops, made by a cooper's long skill. The standard bulk container of Europe from Roman times to the 19th century: wine, ale, salt fish, salt meat, butter, nails, gunpowder [M].

nodes.label: Tin cans
nodes.desc: Food sealed in tinplate (iron sheet coated with tin) with solder, from the 1810s [M]; first for armies and ships. Containers joined tin mining and later steel.

nodes.label: Bast fibre cord
nodes.desc: Cord twisted from lime, nettle or willow bark after retting in water; with sinew, rawhide and withies, the first binding. It made nets, snares, lines and lashing.

nodes.label: Hemp
nodes.desc: A bast fibre crop for rope, sailcloth and sacking; like flax it needed good land, manure and retting water. Navies imported Baltic hemp.

nodes.label: Ropewalk
nodes.desc: A long shed where hemp was laid into rope; capital sunk in one long building. It paid only for navies and merchant fleets.

nodes.label: Baltic bulk trade
nodes.desc: Dutch and English bought Baltic grain, timber, hemp and tar, goods that embodied other people's land. Pomeranz calls such imports 'ghost acres' [M].

nodes.label: Dutch peat fuel economy
nodes.desc: Bog peat cut in spring, dried in summer and moved by canal: stored land, many years of growth in each cut. The Dutch Golden Age ran on it [V] (contested as a sufficient cause); output fell about 20% in the 1660s [V, weakly sourced].

nodes.label: Hydroelectric power
nodes.desc: Electricity from falling water from the 1880s [M]: the mill's site-bound power carried by wire. With wind and solar, the return of place-bound power.

nodes.label: Norfolk four-course rotation
nodes.desc: Wheat, turnips, barley and clover: turnips and clover were both fodder and fertility, so more beasts and more manure. English wheat yields rose about a half in 1800 to 1850 [V].

nodes.label: Marling and liming fields
nodes.desc: Clay-lime marl or burnt lime spread on acid or light soils; it needed pits, kilns and fuel. One of the fertility rungs before mineral fertiliser.

nodes.label: Folding sheep on arable
nodes.place: chalk and sand lands of England
nodes.desc: Sheep penned by night on the fallow inside hurdles of withies, with a shepherd, so their dung fertilised the arable. The fold course tied a lord's flock to tenants' fields.

nodes.label: Town night soil
nodes.desc: Human dung and stable manure carted from towns to fields near them, which made intensive farming possible around cities.

nodes.label: Guano and Chilean nitrate
nodes.desc: Bird dung and mined nitrate shipped across the oceans from the 1840s to the 1910s [M]. They joined fertility to ocean shipping and mining.

nodes.label: Saltpetre
nodes.desc: Nitre from beds of dung and urine and earth scraped from stables, later Indian imports. In Europe gathered under state monopolies (saltpetre men), for gunpowder and curing meat.

nodes.label: Gunpowder
nodes.desc: Saltpetre, charcoal and sulphur. It made charcoal and saltpetre strategic and was shipped in barrels.

nodes.label: Ice houses
nodes.desc: Cool cellars and insulated stores of winter ice, first for the rich, then dairies and fish. The rung before mechanical refrigeration.

nodes.label: Stints on the common
nodes.desc: Limits on how many beasts each holder may put on the common: the answer to arable eating pasture and to overgrazing. Ostrom's commons institutions [M].

nodes.label: Enclosure for sheep
nodes.desc: Arable and commons turned to fenced sheepwalk in 15th- and 16th-century England ('sheep eat men'). Statutes against depopulation failed where wool paid.

nodes.label: Mill, weir and river rules
nodes.desc: Rules for one river with many claims: mill rights, weir laws, fixed fishing times, ordinances on where tanners and retters may work. Mills hold water, fish need runs, tanning and retting foul it.

nodes.label: Wood pasture and pannage
nodes.desc: Grazing beasts and deer under scattered trees, with pigs on the autumn mast (pannage). Browsing kills young regrowth, so wood pasture and coppice exclude each other.

nodes.label: Coppice with standards
nodes.desc: Underwood cut on rotation with oaks left among it to grow to timber over 50 to 150 years. Broadleaf coppice grows about 2.5 t of dry wood a hectare a year (cited); a standard was capital left by grandfathers.

nodes.label: Withies and rods
nodes.desc: Hazel and willow rods on 1 to 10 years: 25,000 to 30,000 rods a hectare from eight- or nine-year hazel (cited). They made wattle, hurdles, fences, baskets, fish traps and weirs.

nodes.label: Oak tanbark
nodes.desc: Oak bark stripped in spring when the sap runs, a pulse in the coppice year; the peeled oak then sold as poles or charcoal wood. It bound the tanner to the oak woods.

nodes.label: Fenced coppice by year
nodes.desc: Woods divided in time (fenced panels by year of cut) and in right (who may take what, when). Restraint enforced by bank, ditch, hedge and calendar, with fines for breaking it.

nodes.label: Naval oak and compass timber
nodes.desc: Navies turned great oak into a strategic good regulated by the state (m); a 74-gun ship took of the order of 2,000 to 3,500 oaks [M, part 01]. A chokepoint created by a later chain on a resource that grows on the scale of a century.

nodes.label: Plantation forestry
nodes.desc: Conifers in even-aged blocks for pit props, pulp and boards: the wood became a crop managed by an owner with machines. The coppice commons fell with the demand that made it worth defending.

nodes.label: Wood pulp
nodes.desc: Wood ground or cooked to fibre for paper and cardboard; with plywood and particleboard, wood as fibre and panel rather than beam (20th c.).

nodes.label: Flint mines
nodes.desc: The first extractive industry: shafts dug through chalk to the floorstone. Grime's Graves had at least 433 shafts over about 37 ha, mostly 2600 to 2300 BC (cited), and may have yielded 16,000 to 18,000 t of flint (rough). Crew work for a place-bound good traded far.

nodes.label: Fire-setting ore mining
nodes.desc: Heat the rock face, quench it, break it with stone mauls and antler picks (m). The first way to mine copper ore.

nodes.label: Arsenical copper
nodes.desc: Copper smelted from mixed ores, often arsenical, which made it harder (m). The bridge between pure copper and tin bronze.

nodes.label: Leather bellows
nodes.desc: A leather bag pumped by hand or foot to blow the furnace and forge; it tied metal to the carcass. Later driven by water wheels.

nodes.label: Long-distance tin trade
nodes.desc: Tin is rare and far from most copper, so bronze needed traders, ships and safe routes. The Uluburun wreck (c.1320 BC) carried 348 ingots, about 10 t of copper and 1 t of tin, a third of the tin traced to Musiston in Uzbekistan (cited). Assembly plus double chokepoint; when the routes broke, the metal failed.

nodes.label: Mining law and free miners
nodes.place: Cornwall stannaries; German Bergregal; Forest of Dean
nodes.desc: A right to a resource separated from ownership of the land: miners staked claims under a special law and paid dues to the crown (m). Chartered rights and royal dues on Cornish and Devon tin.

nodes.label: Mine shares (Kuxe)
nodes.desc: Joint ownership of a mine in parts, an early home of shares and investors (m). Deeper mines needed drainage capital no one miner had.

nodes.label: Mine drainage (adits, pumps)
nodes.desc: As mines went deeper they needed adits, then pumps, then steam (m). Pumping mines was the Newcomen engine's first job, at about 4 kW [M, part 01].

nodes.label: Bog ore and ironstone
nodes.desc: Iron ore is common almost everywhere, so iron ended bronze's double chokepoint. The chokepoint moved from the mine to the woods and the smith.

nodes.label: Village smithy
nodes.desc: Anvil, hearth, bellows, hammers, tongs, a stock of iron and charcoal, and years of skill: the deepest village trade. The village depended on the smith as on the miller; towns split the trade into blacksmiths, locksmiths, farriers, cutlers and more.

nodes.label: Iron-edged tools
nodes.desc: An iron edge on wood: ploughshare, axe, spade, scythe, sickle. It multiplied the labour of every other chain, and the smith's mending kept it working.

nodes.label: Water-powered bloomery and hammer
nodes.desc: A wheel driving bellows and hammer at a bloomery from the 13th century (m): larger blooms, at the lord's or a monastery's mill site.

nodes.label: Cast pig iron
nodes.desc: Liquid iron from the blast furnace, carbon-rich and brittle, good for guns and pots. A charcoal furnace took about 8 t of wood for 2 t of charcoal to smelt 1 t of pig (cited).

nodes.label: Finery forge
nodes.desc: Pig iron refined to bar (wrought) iron under a water hammer, at a second site with more charcoal. The blast furnace and finery made a two-site enterprise.

nodes.label: Ironmaster's woodland leases
nodes.desc: A furnace ran for months on the wood of about a three-mile radius (cited), so the ironmaster leased woods for miles and bought coppice on long rotations; colliers, cutters, carters and founders became a hired crew. The Weald made over 9,000 tons a year in the 1590s (cited).

nodes.label: Crucible steel
nodes.desc: Huntsman's crucible steel of the 1740s (m): small quantities of uniform steel for tools and springs.

nodes.label: Steel rails
nodes.desc: Rails were the first mass market for steel. US rails fell from $174 a ton in 1868 to $17 in 1898 (cited).

nodes.label: Gilchrist Thomas basic process
nodes.desc: A basic lining that took the phosphorus out of the melt (1878) (m), making phosphoric ores in Lorraine and Sweden usable; its slag was sold as fertiliser.

nodes.label: Basic oxygen furnace
nodes.desc: Fast oxygen converters from the 1950s (m), now the main route: about 70% of the 1,883 Mt of crude steel made in 2024 came by blast furnace and basic oxygen (cited).

nodes.label: Steel scrap loop
nodes.desc: Scrap remelted in open hearths and then electric arc furnaces; about 29% of world steel now comes by electric arc, much of it from scrap (cited). The scrap yard is now an ore deposit.

nodes.label: Nailers and cutlers
nodes.desc: Metal trades among the first organised on putting-out lines (m): a merchant's iron worked at home by the piece.

nodes.label: Machine-made nails
nodes.desc: Nails cut by machine rather than forged by hand (18th to 19th c.) (m); with sawmills they made the balloon frame possible.

nodes.label: Cupellation
nodes.desc: Silver separated from lead ore by oxidising the lead away in a hearth of bone ash (m). So silver mining was a lead industry with a precious by-product.

nodes.label: Silver mining towns
nodes.desc: The great silver strikes made mining towns with their own law (m). Coin made from their silver fed every other chain's exchange.

nodes.label: Huancavelica mercury
nodes.desc: The mercury mine that fed Potosi's refining. With Potosi it put out more than a quarter of the mercury vapour emitted in Latin America from 1500 to 1800 (cited).

nodes.label: Mita labour draft
nodes.desc: A colonial draft that took about one in seven able-bodied men of the subject districts each year for the mines (cited). Coerced labour where the capital needed more hands than wages could draw.

nodes.label: Potosi patio silver
nodes.desc: After 1572 Potosi's ores were refined by mercury amalgamation (patio) with mita labour (cited): chokepoint at the lode, assembly of ore, mercury, salt, fuel and labour. Its share of world silver is contested: 60 to 80% in the late 16th century by some estimates (contested).

nodes.label: Timber frame
nodes.desc: Standards felled, hewn and jointed by the carpenter on a framing yard, then raised by a crew; infill of wattle and daub. Grundle House used about 330 mostly small, young oaks (m), so building fit the coppice-with-standards.

nodes.label: Saw pit
nodes.desc: A pair of sawyers, one above and one in the pit, ripping timber into boards. Worked wood (boards, staves, poles) went into building, barrels, carts, ploughs and boats.

nodes.label: Lime mortar
nodes.desc: Quicklime slaked and mixed with sand. The lime kiln was a hub: rock, fuel, building, farming and leather in one fitting.

nodes.label: Mason crews and lodges
nodes.place: cathedral works of England and France
nodes.desc: Itinerant crews of rough masons and freemasons moving between large works under a master, paid by the day. A stone church or castle took years and hundreds of workers (rough).

nodes.label: Thatch
nodes.desc: Straw (a by-product of grain, 15 to 30 years) or water reed (up to about 50) (m). The cheapest roof and the worst fire risk.

nodes.label: Clay roof tiles
nodes.place: Greece; later towns of northern Europe
nodes.desc: Clay fired in a kiln: dear but fire-resistant. Fuel-bound with increasing returns, like brick.

nodes.label: Town fire regulations
nodes.desc: After London's fire of 1212, fitz Ailwin's rules banned new roofs of reed, rush or straw (widely flouted); after 1666, when about 13,200 houses burned, the rebuilding acts required brick and stone (m). One house's thatch threatens the street, so the rule had to be collective.

nodes.label: Great rebuilding in brick
nodes.desc: Houses rebuilt in brick and stone with chimneys, glazing and upper floors in the 16th and 17th centuries (m); brick became a mass good.

nodes.label: Balloon frame
nodes.desc: Light sawn timber nailed together with no joinery: housing as a mass product. It needed sawmills and machine-made nails.

nodes.label: Reinforced concrete
nodes.desc: Steel and cement fused into one material (1860s to 1890s) (m). Cement now emits about 1.56 Gt of CO2 a year (2023), 5 to 8% of the world's, 60% of it from calcination (cited): the lime kiln at planetary scale.

nodes.label: English raw wool exports
nodes.desc: England's chief export: about 25,000 sacks in 1280, peaking at 40,000 to 45,000 a year, down to about 9,700 by 1476 as cloth took its place (secondary summary of Carus-Wilson and Coleman).

nodes.label: English broadcloth exports
nodes.desc: England wove its own wool: cloth exports rose from about 10,000 a year in 1349-50 to about 140,000 in 1539-40 (secondary summary). A sack of wool made about 4.3 broadcloths.

nodes.label: Spinning wheel
nodes.desc: Faster spinning than distaff and spindle, which managed 40 to 100 m of yarn an hour (cited); guilds sometimes banned wheel yarn for warps at first (m). Spinning was the bottleneck of cloth and the main paid work of women.

nodes.label: Horizontal treadle loom
nodes.desc: A foot-worked loom of the high Middle Ages (m) that took weaving out of the household into men's workshops in towns. A loom is capital; efficient weaving used two looms and two weavers.

nodes.label: Alum mordant
nodes.desc: The mordant that fixed dyes, also used in tawing; a traded chokepoint of the dyer's assembly.

nodes.label: Woad, madder and weld
nodes.desc: Field-grown plant dyes (blue, red, yellow) often carried far to the dyer. Displaced by coal-tar dyes from the 1850s.

nodes.label: Retting ponds
nodes.desc: Flax and hemp stems rotted in water for days to free the fibre, fouling the water and killing fish downstream. A water conflict at one step of the linen chain.

nodes.label: Linen bleachfields
nodes.desc: Linen laid out in the sun for weeks with lye: a seasonal pulse at the end of the flax chain.

nodes.label: Flying shuttle
nodes.desc: Kay's shuttle (1733) (m) doubled the weaver's speed and sharpened the shortage of yarn.

nodes.label: Spinning mule
nodes.desc: Crompton's mule (1779) (m) had 48 spindles and spun about a pound of fine 60s yarn a day (cited). It attacked the spinning bottleneck of the whole cloth chain.

nodes.label: Self-acting mule
nodes.desc: Roberts's automatic mule (patents 1825, 1830) spun about 900 hanks a machine a day against about 25 for a jenny and 8 for a hand wheel (cited). Hours to spin 100 lb of cotton fell from about 50,000 by hand to about 135 (m, contested).

nodes.label: Indian handloom cotton
nodes.desc: Hand-spun, handwoven Indian cotton cloth that supplied the Indian Ocean trade; mill-spun cotton displaced it after the 1770s.

nodes.label: Coal-tar dyes
nodes.desc: Synthetic dyes from coal tar from the 1850s (m); they ended the plant-dye trades and merged cloth with chemistry.

nodes.label: Rayon
nodes.desc: Regenerated cellulose fibre made from wood pulp (m): the first fibre from a chemical works rather than a field or flock.

nodes.label: Global garment chain
nodes.place: Bangladesh, China and brands' home countries
nodes.desc: Fibre plants, mills, dye houses and cut-and-sew workshops in low-wage countries, the brand owning design and market: putting-out made global. World fibre was about 132 Mt in 2024, polyester 59% (cited); Rana Plaza (2013) killed over 1,100 garment workers (m).

nodes.label: Carcass joint products
nodes.desc: A slaughtered beast gives meat, hide, fat, horn, bone, sinew, guts and dung at once; the butcher's leftovers fed half a dozen trades, zoned by smell in the medieval town. About half of a modern meat animal is not eaten (cited).

nodes.label: Horn, bone and glue trades
nodes.desc: Horners, bone-workers and glue-boilers: combs, lantern panes, handles, dice, needles, glue and size from the carcass's leftovers. Bone ash also lined the cupellation hearth.

nodes.label: Parchment
nodes.desc: Limed and scraped skins of sheep, goats and calves for writing; a branch of the carcass chain.

nodes.label: Currying and leather guilds
nodes.desc: Shaving, oiling with tallow or fish oil, and finishing the tanned hide. Curriers and cordwainers were separate guilds from tanners and fought over who did which step (m): trades formed round the steps of one chain.

nodes.label: Tawing (alum leather)
nodes.desc: White leather made quickly with alum and salt, and oil tanning (chamois) with fish oil (m): the faster, lighter substitutes to bark tanning for gloves and fine goods.

nodes.label: Tannin extracts
nodes.desc: Imported quebracho and chestnut extracts in the 19th century (m) freed tanning from local bark.

nodes.label: Chrome tanning
nodes.desc: Described by Knapp in 1858, commercial from about 1878, patented in the US 1884 (cited): tanning in days instead of the 11 to 18 months of bark (cited). About 80% of leather is now chrome-tanned; leather moved from the woods to the chemical works.

nodes.label: Industrial rendering
nodes.desc: Everything not eaten gathered into one plant: fats, proteins and meals for feed, pet food, soap, oleochemicals, biodiesel and fertiliser. North American rendering takes about 27.5 Mt of raw material a year (cited). By-product capture completed.

nodes.label: Wicker fish traps
nodes.desc: Eel baskets and traps woven of withies in a few days: the coppice into the water.

nodes.label: Fishing nets
nodes.desc: Seines and drift nets of flax or hemp cord, many hours of netting: a long skill.

nodes.label: Fish weir
nodes.desc: Stakes, wattle and stones across a river, taking a share of every run and blocking boats and the fish of those upstream. Magna Carta ordered weirs removed from the Thames and Medway (m).

nodes.label: Fishponds and stews
nodes.desc: Dug ponds with dams and sluices, 'living larders' of high-status sites: keeping instead of catching.

nodes.label: Salt herring and cod
nodes.desc: Fish packed in salt and barrels, the staple of fast days across Europe [M, part 01]. An assembly with salt as its chokepoint.

nodes.label: Scania herring fair
nodes.desc: The medieval Baltic herring market where the Hanse packed herring in Luneburg salt (m).

nodes.label: Stockfish
nodes.desc: Cod dried in wind without salt, from Norway and Iceland (m): a long-distance commodity carried with grain.

nodes.label: Dutch herring buss
nodes.desc: A decked vessel of about 15 crew on a 50 ft keel that gutted and salted herring at sea in barrels, so it could stay out for weeks (cited); fleets of 400 to 500 (cited). Its assembly (Biscay salt, barrels, hemp nets, Baltic timber) tied the Dutch economy to half of Europe.

nodes.label: Steam trawler
nodes.desc: Steam trawlers and the otter trawl of the 1880s to 1890s (m): the seabed swept, fishing a capital fleet with wage crews.

nodes.label: Ice and the fish train
nodes.desc: Ice and railways in the 19th century (m) carried fresh fish to inland cities.

nodes.label: Freezer factory trawler
nodes.desc: Diesel, sonar, synthetic nets and freezers in the 20th century (m): distant-water fleets with catches far beyond the fish's recovery.

nodes.label: Northern cod moratorium
nodes.desc: Harvestable northern cod fell 82% from 1962 to 1977 and the spawning stock was about 1% of its peak by 1992; the moratorium of 2 July 1992 put 30,000 to 40,000 people out of work (cited). The weir and the commons at the scale of an ocean.

nodes.label: Exclusive economic zones
nodes.desc: The sea enclosed by states in the 1970s and 1980s (m).

nodes.label: Tradable fishing quotas
nodes.desc: Late 20th-century quotas and tradable shares (m): the commons privatised as rights to a share of the catch.

nodes.label: Aquaculture
nodes.desc: Keeping instead of catching at scale: in 2022 aquaculture overtook capture for aquatic animals, 94.4 Mt against 92.3 Mt (cited), growing about 5% a year since 2000. The medieval fishpond became the dominant form.

nodes.label: Royal forest law
nodes.desc: Crown law over whole districts protecting deer and their cover, with its own courts (m): a chokepoint made by law.

nodes.label: Deer park
nodes.desc: Deer fed, guarded and culled inside a pale of fence, bank and hedge: about 3,200 parks by 1300, some 2% of England (cited). Capital sunk in the pale, enforced by law and keepers.

nodes.label: Rabbit warren
nodes.desc: Rabbits introduced by the Normans by about 1100 and kept in guarded, often leased warrens for meat and fur (cited); a luxury in the 13th century, a common pest by the 19th (m).

nodes.label: Poaching and game laws
nodes.desc: The peasant snared and poached for food and was punished for it: the contest over a commons that law took away. Later game laws and gamekeepers guarded the shooting estate (m).

nodes.label: North American fur trade
nodes.desc: Commercial trapping for European markets (m): a global chain from the hunt to the hatter.
